#India's oil imports from Saudi Arabia exceeded those from the United Arab Emirates in October for the first time since the Iran war disrupted regional supplies, trade data showed, as Riyadh offered discounted cargoes to regain market share.

Russia remained India's top oil supplier in October, followed by Saudi Arabia and the UAE, the data showed.

Saudi imports rose to an eight-month high of about 790,000 barrels per day (bpd), while purchases from the UAE fell to a seven-month low of 612,000 bpd. #oott https://t.co/z6x9FCZClS

#China’s appetite for crude is recovering faster than expected in the final months of 2026, as lower oil prices push cash-strapped refiners to use up government-granted import allowances and encourage processors to rebuild stockpiles depleted by months of war.

Energy Aspects and FGE NexantECA have raised fourth-quarter import forecasts to 10.1 million and 10.2 million barrels a day respectively, while Rystad Energy increased its estimate to 9.8 million.

The figures are heading closer to China’s average of 11.6 million barrels a day in 2025, when the country was taking advantage of cheap prices to build up strategic and commercial inventories, and mark a significant rebound from June’s lows of 7.15 million. #oott https://t.co/66xZAxdN2k

The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index (BBDXY) has extended its breakout earlier this month to reach its highest level since April 2025, supported by rising US Treasury yields and growing expectations of further Fed rate hikes. Hawkish FOMC minutes and comments from Governor Waller have reinforced this shift, driving broad-based dollar strength and tightening global financial conditions. The impact has been particularly pronounced among commodity-linked currencies, with the Norwegian krone and Australian dollar both losing more than 4.5% month-to-date.

Beyond higher yields and a more hawkish Fed outlook, the dollar's strength may also reflect tightening global liquidity and rising demand for cash. AI-related financing requirements, IPO activity, equity market volatility and elevated energy security costs are potentially adding to dollar funding needs just as higher interest rates make financing more expensive. This combination risks creating a self-reinforcing cycle of dollar strength, tighter financial conditions and reduced risk appetite. These development being one of the drivers behind the ongoing correction across commodities.

What could reverse the trend? A sustained moderation in US inflation, potentially helped by the recent decline in crude oil and fuel prices, would be an important catalyst. Evidence that inflation is rolling over could ease expectations for further Fed rate hikes, bring Treasury yields lower and reduce the dollar's interest-rate advantage. EIA crude oil and fuel inventory report: US crude oil, gasoline and distillate inventories all rose last week, pointing to a gradual normalisation of supply conditions. Gasoline stocks are rebuilding rapidly amid seasonally weaker demand, while crude and distillate inventories remain below their five-year averages, with the latter still highlighting underlying tightness in the fuel market. Meanwhile, US crude production reached a fresh record of 14.03 million barrels per day, while oil exports rebounded above 4 million barrels per day. Refinery demand also remains elevated for this time of year, supporting fuel production and inventory replenishment. Overall, the report reinforces a picture of improving supply availability and easing market tightness, although historically low distillate stocks continue to provide a degree of support to refined product prices.

#Commodities - AM note from Copenhagen:

#Copper slumped 5% yesterday to a seven-month low, pressured by global growth concerns, disappointing Chinese demand signals and expectations of increased US exports. Negative sentiment at a major industry conference in Shanghai triggered heavy speculative selling, while reports that copper could be redirected to China in December eased concerns about tight local supplies. Despite the sharp selloff, the longer-term outlook remains supported by tight scrap and mine supplies, resilient infrastructure demand and committed AI-related investment.

Precious metals: Gold extended its recent slump, touching a fresh 15-month low of USD 3,694 in Asia, as hawkish Fed minutes and Governor Waller's comments reinforced expectations of further rate hikes. Beyond higher yields and rate hike concerns, the broader commodity selloff may also reflect tightening global dollar liquidity as the dollar continues to rally. Rising AI-related financing needs, IPO activity, equity market volatility and elevated energy security costs are increasing demand for cash just as higher interest rates make funding more expensive. Gold, given its deep liquidity, and other metals may therefore be caught in a broader dash for cash, with investors selling liquid assets to meet funding needs and reduce risk exposure.

Oil: Brent trades near unchanged around USD 92 after falling 1.3% on the Wednesday. Alongside broader risk reduction across commodities, recent weakness has been driven by recovering Middle East production and exports, renewing concerns about an emerging supply glut. However, the risk of fresh disruptions remains, with the New York Times reporting that Trump, under renewed pressure from Israel's Netanyahu, is considering fresh strikes against Iran. Tehran has responded by warning neighbouring countries of retaliation should they allow US attacks to be launched from their territory.
